extracted.intended_audience: students, mathematicians, logicians, and philosophers interested in foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A general encyclopedic survey of the aims, historical development, major approaches, and desiderata for foundations of mathematics (axiomatic set theory, type theory, formalism, intuitionism, etc.). Suitable as an introduction for readers seeking the main standards and problems in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational goal: consistency and reliable concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations of mathematics are the logical and mathematical frameworks that allow the development of mathematics without generating self-contradictory theories, and to have reliable concepts of theorems, proofs, algorithms, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations should prevent self-contradiction and provide stable meanings for notions like theorem, proof, and algorithm; this motivates formal axiomatic frameworks and metamathematical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-from-axioms requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical assertion is considered as truth only if it is a theorem that is proved from true premises by means of a sequence of syllogisms (inference rules), the premises being either already proved theorems or self-evident assertions called axioms or postulates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises the axiomatic method: statements accepted as mathematical truth should be derivable via explicit inference rules from specified axioms or previously proven theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic method
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiomatic method: the proof of a theorem must result from explicit axioms and previously proved theorems by the application of clearly defined inference rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms need not correspond to physical reality; selection of axioms is guided by their ability to support rich, useful theories. Use of axiomatic formalization underlies modern foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Frege pointed out consistency (impossibility of proving contradictory statements) as a desired property of a logical theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational systems are evaluated on whether they avoid internal contradictions (e.g., Russell's paradox motivated axiomatic set theories). Note Gödel limits on proving consistency from within sufficiently strong systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (as a desideratum for logical theories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frege listed completeness (any statement is either provable or refutable; that is, its negation is provable) as a desired property of a logical theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is an ideal: first-order logic has the semantic completeness theorem (provability iff truth in all models) but formal theories containing arithmetic cannot be both complete and sufficiently expressive (Gödel incompleteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frege listed decidability (there is a decision procedure to test every statement) as a desired property of a logical theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many foundational questions are undecidable in general (Entscheidungsproblem, halting problem); validity in first-order logic is not decidable though it is semi-decidable. Decidability is therefore a key practical criterion but often unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (ZFC) as standard foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC) is the standard foundation of modern mathematics and is generally used implicitly unless otherwise specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of ZFC is the de facto standard for formalizing mathematics; many results and practice assume ZFC. Its consistency cannot be proved within itself (Gödel), but it was designed to avoid paradoxes like Russell's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-theoretic and other non-set-theoretic foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Type theory (including intuitionistic type theory and calculus of constructions) and approaches like univalent foundations/homotopy type theory and topos-theoretic foundations are alternatives to set-theoretic foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type-theoretic foundations are increasingly used in proof assistants; they provide different tradeoffs (e.g., different ways to compare consistency strength and different tooling for formal proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist/intuitionist proof requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitionists require proofs to be 'constructive' in nature – the existence of an object must be demonstrated rather than inferred from a demonstration of the impossibility of its non-existence. For example, reductio ad absurdum is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under constructivist standards, non-constructive existence proofs are considered invalid; systems and theorems are evaluated by whether they admit constructive proofs and constructive interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalism: syntactic criterion of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalists (exemplified by Hilbert) consider that a theorem is true if it can be derived from the axioms of a formal system using rules of formal logic; mathematics is treated as a system of symbol manipulation governed by definite rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalism evaluates mathematical correctness by formal derivability. It shifts focus from 'truth' of axioms to the internal formal properties of systems (consistency, derivability). Hilbert aimed to show consistency by finitary means, but Gödel set limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatization of natural numbers (Peano axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peano axioms provide a complete axiomatisation based on the ordinal property of natural numbers; the axioms involve quantification over infinite sets and are thus second-order in flavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations must account for natural numbers rigorously; choices about first- vs second-order formulations have implications for expressiveness and meta-theoretic issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness property for real numbers (least upper bound / Cauchy limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The completeness of the real numbers (e.g., 'every subset of the real numbers that is bounded has a least upper bound' or every Cauchy sequence has a real limit) is essential to rigorous analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of real numbers (Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences) and the completeness axiom are evaluation criteria for foundations of analysis; formalizing completeness often requires quantification over infinite sets and motivates higher-order considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of paradoxes via axiomatization (e.g., Russell's paradox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradoxes such as Russell's paradox showed naive set theory to be self-contradictory; resolving such paradoxes motivated axiomatic set theories like ZF and ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foundational framework is judged by how it prevents known paradoxes (through careful axioms and restrictions) and whether it provides principled responses to independence results and paradoxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of metamathematical limitations (Gödel's incompleteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that any sufficiently powerful recursively axiomatizable system containing arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency and will have true statements unprovable within the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational proposals must account for these intrinsic limits: no system meeting certain strength criteria can achieve all desiderata (consistency proof internally, completeness). This shapes realistic goals (e.g., partial completion of Hilbert's program, relative consistency proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness and semantic completeness (as meta-properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's completeness theorem: in first-order logic there is an equivalence between formal provability of a formula and its truth in all possible models (semantic completeness); soundness is the impossibility of proving false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational systems and logics are evaluated by soundness (only proving semantically valid statements) and, where applicable, by completeness results linking provability and model-theoretic truth. Practical consequences include semi-decidability of consistency checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability / (un)decidability of theories and problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Key metatheorems: the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable in general; Turing proved the halting problem is undecidable; validity in first-order logic is not decidable (only semi-decidable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations are assessed for which fragments or theories are decidable, semi-decidable, or undecidable; this has implications for algorithmic reasoning and the scope of automated proof systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical selection of axioms: usefulness and mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of axioms is often guided by usefulness, mathematical intuition, and the ability to support rich, interesting theories rather than by correspondence to physical reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations are evaluated partly on pragmatic grounds: whether the chosen axioms enable productive development of mathematics, guide intuition, and integrate with mainstream mathematical practice (e.g., acceptance of ZFC by most mathematicians).
